packet.headline_seed: Do it at home too, women tell Japanese fans who cleaned World Cup stadium
packet.description_seed: Some see a double standard: Japanese men who clean in public while their wives do all the housework.

what: Do it at home too, women tell Japanese fans who cleaned World Cup stadium

clean_source_blocks.text: For years, Japanese football fans have won praise for cleaning up stadiums after World Cup matches. But this time, they're catching heat at home. When photos emerged this week of Japanese fans combing the stands with trash bags after a match, some saw a double standard: men who clean after themselves in public while leaving the burden at home to their wives. A Japanese poster went viral soon after, juxtaposing a man picking litter at the stadium with the same guy reclined on a sofa at home, using his phone near a basket of laundry while his wife did the dishes. Men in Japan should "pitch in more at home" as their time spent doing chores is among the shortest in the world, the poster text read. That post has been liked 60,000 times on X.
Some see a double standard: Japanese men who clean in public while their wives do all the housework.

This disparity is especially pronounced in young families. A government survey from 2021 found that in dual-income households with children under six years old, women spend more than seven hours a day on household chores while men spend less than two hours. Some social media users have also taken issue with what they see as the hypocrisy of picking up rubbish abroad, when Japan's public spaces are often lined with rubbish after large events. But as the debate over the division of housework rages, many argue that Japanese fans' signature stadium cleanups should be encouraged, not nitpicked at. "Where's the embarrassment in that?" an X user wrote. "It's way better than reports saying 'Japanese people are littering abroad.'" Such cleanups appear to have influenced fans from other countries too.

"Everyone wants to save the world, but no one wants to help mom do the dishes," an X user commented, referencing a quote by American author PJ O'Rourke. "There's probably a guy among these people picking up trash, who has a young kid at home and left his wife to look after them to come watch the World Cup," wrote another. Cleanliness and cleaning up after oneself in public places is deeply ingrained in Japanese culture. In terms of time spent doing housework, however, Japanese men rank the lowest among highly-developed countries. According Organisation of Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) data from 2021, Japanese women spend more than three hours per day on unpaid work - more than five times that of men, who clock 47 minutes a day.

[Lähde: Yahoo Sports]
The stands and seats following most sporting events are usually atrocious. Between plastic cups, used napkins, and food containers left behind, most people leave their trash for stadium employees to pick up after them.

But this commonplace behavior is simply unheard of in Japanese culture. Japanese World Cup fans in the United States are showing the world how courteous they are by cleaning up after themselves after the game.

Clips of Japanese soccer fans have recently made headlines, showing fans collecting trash in blue garbage bags following their country's first World Cup match between Japan and the Netherlands on Sunday, June 14. Their selfless act is having an impact on people around the world.

Japanese fans carried blue bags with them to celebrate during the match against the Netherlands. But once the game was over, they immediately put them to use as trash bags.

In a video shared by FIFA, one Japanese fan cleaning up explained why they think it's important to do so.

"That's the culture. It's respect for everything," the fan said. "Respect for the players, supporters, and also for the stadium. We are honored to be here, so we don't want to make a mess and then leave it. I think that's the reason why we're doing it."

However, it wasn't just Japanese fans who tidied up. The Japan national football team (also called the "Samurai Blue") did its part in the locker room.

"Chairs were stacked, trash was collected, and towels were left neatly folded in the center of the room," according to KDFW-TV. "The pink and orange bibs that players and coaches wore to indicate their stadium clearance were stacked by the door."

Japanese fans have practiced cleaning up stadiums after World Cup games since they played their first match in 1998, according to The Associated Press. Back then, Japanese soccer fans collected trash following World Cup games in France. Ever since, they've continued to do so.

payload.title: Japanilaisfanien stadionin siivous herätti kotimaassa keskustelun kotitöistä
payload.summary: Japanilaiset jalkapallofanit ovat saaneet vuosien ajan kiitosta katsomoiden siivoamisesta MM-otteluiden jälkeen. Tuore keskustelu on kuitenkin kääntänyt huomion siihen, jakautuvatko siivous ja muut kotityöt Japanissa tasapuolisesti myös kotona.
payload.content:
Japanilaiset jalkapallofanit ovat jälleen nousseet esiin siivottuaan katsomoita MM-ottelun jälkeen, mutta tällä kertaa tuttu kiitoksen aihe on synnyttänyt myös arvostelua Japanissa. Sosiaalisessa mediassa osa keskustelijoista on pitänyt toimintaa esimerkkinä kaksijakoisuudesta: julkisella paikalla siivotaan näkyvästi, mutta kotona suuri osa kotitöistä jää yhä naisille.

## Julkinen siisteys ja kodin arki törmäsivät keskustelussa

Japanilaisfanien tapa kerätä roskia otteluiden jälkeen on ollut kansainvälisesti tunnettu jo vuosia. Tuoreiden kuvien levittyä tällä viikolla keskustelu sai kuitenkin uuden sävyn, kun japanilainen julkaisu rinnasti stadionilla roskia keräävän miehen kotona sohvalla puhelintaan käyttävään mieheen. Kuvassa vaimo hoitaa tiskit ja pyykkikori odottaa vieressä.

Julkaisun viesti oli, että japanilaisten miesten pitäisi osallistua kotitöihin enemmän. Se sai X-palvelussa kymmeniätuhansia tykkäyksiä. Kommentoijat viittasivat siihen, että julkinen siisteys voi näyttää hyveelliseltä, jos sama vastuu ei jatku perhe-elämässä.

## Tilastot kertovat suuresta erosta

Keskustelua on vahvistanut tieto kotitöiden epätasaisesta jakautumisesta. Japanin hallituksen vuonna 2021 tekemän selvityksen mukaan kahden työssäkäyvän vanhemman perheissä, joissa on alle kuusivuotiaita lapsia, naiset käyttävät kotitöihin yli seitsemän tuntia päivässä. Miehillä vastaava aika jää alle kahteen tuntiin.

Myös OECD:n vuoden 2021 tietojen mukaan japanilaiset miehet tekevät hyvin vähän palkatonta työtä verrattuna naisiin. Japanilaiset naiset käyttävät palkattomaan työhön yli kolme tuntia päivässä, kun miesten aika on 47 minuuttia.

## Kaikki eivät halua moittia stadionien siivoojia

Osa keskustelijoista on silti puolustanut fanien toimintaa. Heidän mukaansa katsomoiden siivoaminen ulkomailla on parempi kuva Japanista kuin välinpitämätön roskaaminen. Siisteys ja omien jälkien korjaaminen julkisissa tiloissa ovat Japanissa vahvoja kulttuurisia käytäntöjä, ja stadionisiivousten on kerrottu vaikuttaneen myös muiden maiden faneihin.

Keskustelun ydin ei siksi ole pelkästään se, pitäisikö fanien kerätä roskia otteluiden jälkeen. Se on laajentunut kysymykseksi siitä, näkyykö sama vastuuntunto myös kotona, missä arjen siivous, lastenhoito ja muu palkaton työ jakautuvat yhä hyvin epätasaisesti.
summary_bullets: Japanilaisfanien stadionien siivoaminen on herättänyt Japanissa myös arvostelua.
Keskustelu liittyy siihen, että kotityöt jakautuvat Japanissa yhä voimakkaasti naisten vastuulle.
Vuoden 2021 tietojen mukaan japanilaiset miehet käyttävät palkattomaan työhön selvästi vähemmän aikaa kuin naiset.

article.journalist_note: Artikkeli perustuu packetin BBC-aineistoon ja rajaa väitteet siinä mainittuihin sosiaalisen median reaktioihin sekä vuoden 2021 hallitus- ja OECD-tietoihin.
article.source_text:
For years, Japanese football fans have won praise for cleaning up stadiums after World Cup matches. But this time, they're catching heat at home. When photos emerged this week of Japanese fans combing the stands with trash bags after a match, some saw a double standard: men who clean after themselves in public while leaving the burden at home to their wives. A Japanese poster went viral soon after, juxtaposing a man picking litter at the stadium with the same guy reclined on a sofa at home, using his phone near a basket of laundry while his wife did the dishes. Men in Japan should "pitch in more at home" as their time spent doing chores is among the shortest in the world, the poster text read. That post has been liked 60,000 times on X.

Some see a double standard: Japanese men who clean in public while their wives do all the housework.

This disparity is especially pronounced in young families. A government survey from 2021 found that in dual-income households with children under six years old, women spend more than seven hours a day on household chores while men spend less than two hours. Some social media users have also taken issue with what they see as the hypocrisy of picking up rubbish abroad, when Japan's public spaces are often lined with rubbish after large events. But as the debate over the division of housework rages, many argue that Japanese fans' signature stadium cleanups should be encouraged, not nitpicked at. "Where's the embarrassment in that?" an X user wrote. "It's way better than reports saying 'Japanese people are littering abroad.'" Such cleanups appear to have influenced fans from other countries too.

"Everyone wants to save the world, but no one wants to help mom do the dishes," an X user commented, referencing a quote by American author PJ O'Rourke. "There's probably a guy among these people picking up trash, who has a young kid at home and left his wife to look after them to come watch the World Cup," wrote another. Cleanliness and cleaning up after oneself in public places is deeply ingrained in Japanese culture. In terms of time spent doing housework, however, Japanese men rank the lowest among highly-developed countries. According Organisation of Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) data from 2021, Japanese women spend more than three hours per day on unpaid work - more than five times that of men, who clock 47 minutes a day.
